the effects of chronic stress in female CRF-OEs, which are characterized by a higher susceptibility to stress-related diseases, including irritable bowel syndrome, and provides a new model of chronic stress-induced colonic dysfunction.

chronic stress, as a result of continuous CRF overdrive in the central nervous system, enhances the pelvic and locomotor responses to superimposition of mild stressors, and the enhanced colonic response is mediated by CRF(1).

the chronic stress, due in part to continuous central CRFs overdrive, renders the CRF-OE females to be more susceptible to superimposed acute stressors, as evidenced by the enhanced colonic, urinary and altered locomotor responses to mild stressors.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
chronic stress in female CRF-OEs, but not male CRF-OEs or wild-type mice, leads to enhanced colonic and altered urinary responses to mild stressors.
CRF(2)-induced colonic response is a protective response to counterbalance CRF-induced visceral hyperalgesia and that this protective response may not be effective in males.
CRF-OE mouse is a useful animal model for studying the impact of chronic stress on the gut and the pelvic functions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
CRF(2)-initiated colono-vaginal response may be an important component of the stress-induced visceral dysfunction.
